What killed Pretoria’s football factory?

By: Matuba Mahlatjie | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Arcadia Shepherds Football Club – produced legends, racially integrated. National talent incubator. Now lies in ruins, homeless people live there. Used to be a beautiful place

Summary:
Arcadia Shepherds was a national talent incubator that produced legends like Mark Fish and Edward Motale. Today, its grounds are a derelict ruin. What forces – financial, political, societal – conspired to destroy South Africa’s most potent unofficial development machine? This is the mystery we will solve.

Further information:
The Investigative Journey We Will Take the Viewer On
1. The Crime Scene: A Factory in Ruins

We open at the Caledonian Stadium. Through stark drone shots, we show the viewer the "body"—the overgrown fields and crumbling structures. This is the factory floor, now silent.

The Question Posed Visually: How did this place, which assembled Bafana Bafana stars, end up like this?

2. The Blueprint: How the Factory Worked

We showcase the "Golden Age" with rich archives and nostalgic interviews.

The Architect: Coach Steve Coetzee explains his methods and his eye for talent.

The Products: Exclusive interviews with Edward Motale (1996 Afcon winner) and former goalkeeper Deshi Bhaktawer. They are living proof of the factory's output, testifying to the unique environment that created them.

The Defiance: We highlight the pioneering signing of Vincent Julius and the visual evolution of the team, showing a club ahead of its time.

3. The Investigation: Who or What Killed the Factory?
This is the core of our investigation, providing concrete answers to the central question.

Suspect 1: Political Sabotage: The fateful Kaiser Chiefs match that gave the apartheid government a pretext to close their ground. Steve Coetzee explicitly identifies this as the beginning of the end.

Suspect 2: Administrative Failure: The decision by club leadership to sell out to Dynamos, despite players offering to play for free. This points to internal failure and a loss of vision.

Suspect 3: Systemic Neglect: We bring in Fran Hilton-Smith, former SAFA Technical Director. She provides the expert, systemic perspective on why grassroots incubators like Arcadia were allowed to die and what this says about the failures of the official development structure.

4. The Verdict: The Legacy of a Lost Factory

We return to the ruins of the Caledonian. The visuals now carry the weight of the answers we've uncovered.

We see Steve Coetzee, now a CAF/SAFA coach educator, trying to rebuild a similar model with his new club, Capital City—a small, hopeful effort against a tide of systemic challenges.

The Final Answer: The factory was killed by a combination of political pressure, internal mismanagement, and a system that failed to protect its most valuable assets. Its death left a hole in South Africa's football soul.

Script:


SCRIPT: What Killed Pretoria’s Football Factory

CLAIRE (VO):
In 1996, South African football was at the pinnacle of its success. Bafana Bafana were African champions. The future was limitless.
(VISUALS: The vibrant archive images from 1996 suddenly cut to a stark, slow-motion drone shot over the derelict, overgrown Caledonian Stadium. The sound of the 1996 cheers fades into an eerie silence.)
CLAIRE (VO):
But that golden era didn't last. The pipeline of world-class talent began to dry up.
(BACK TO BACK UPSOUNDS)
STEVE COETSEE INTERVIEW
00:18:09,666 → 00:18:27,300
We need better coach education and mentorship.

00:12:15,466 – 00:12:27,500
Deshi: We lacked spark, new ideas, new people, which never came. All of that set us back terribly.

CLAIRE (VO):
It’s a depressing metaphor for the state of the sport: once the champions of the African Cup of Nations, South Africa has failed to qualify for three World Cups until now. To understand the fall of a national team, you often have to trace it back to the roots.

STEVEN COETSEE INTERVIEW
00:08:16,100 → 00:08:26,400
Claire: The Caledonian today — you said you drive past it and don’t even want to look at it. Why is that?
00:08:27,166 → 00:08:32,500
Steve: Because it meant so much to all of us.

CLAIRE (VO):
That’s the grassroots factory where stars were made that now lies in ruins.
Claire PTC
We did ask for permission to shoot inside the Caledonian Stadium, but the city of Tshwane refused us entry. They’re saying it’s a construction site, but there is no construction happening. And I can’t see evidence of any construction.

CLAIRE (VO):
In 2014, the city itself approved a plan to upgrade and transform the stadium into a theme park and community hub. But those plans were halted by budget constraints and political infighting. – another promise, broken, leaving the stadium in a state of perpetual decay.

FRAN HILTON-SMITH INTERVIEW
Well, I think, you know, it’s happened a lot around sports centres — with changes in municipalities, changes in government. You get people who are really not interested in sport, who don’t have that feeling, that vibe about keeping things that were really important. And they go to rack and ruin, which is what happened with the Caledonian.


[breather]


CLAIRE (VO):
For decades, the Caledonian Stadium was home to Arcadia Shepherds - and the heart of Coach Steve Coetsee’s football factory. And he says a single game back in 1985 sparked trouble for the stadium.

STEVE COETSEE/ARCADIA SHEPHERDS FORMER COACH INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:09:06,433 → 00:09:13,333
Claire: What would you say was the beginning of the end for the Caledonian? Would you mark it as that Kaizer Chiefs game?
Steve: I think that was the main factor.

CLAIRE (VO):
Arcadia Shepherds hosted a racially-integrated match against Kaizer Chiefs in 1985.
STEVE INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:00:29,566 → 00:00:32,833
Steve: I think people have to understand, in those days. Kaizer Chiefs... have a following of hundreds of thousands... the place was packed. It was quite frightening, actually.
In apartheid South Africa, this was an act of defiance.
And the authorities used the chaos as a pretext to target the club.

STEVE COETSEE INTERVIEW
Finances became a problem, and eventually, the club had to be sold. Every single player said, “We’ll play for nothing.” But it wasn’t to be. The city council refused to return the stadium to Arcadia.

(The Golden Age: Defiance & Unity)


CLAIRE (VO):
But to understand the true cost of that loss, you have to understand what Arcadia was at its peak. It was more than a club; it was a quiet revolution.

STEVE INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:05:08,400 → 00:05:19,133
Football became multiracial in the 70s, long before SAFA. Clubs like Arcadia Shepherds and Wits University had non-white players.

CLAIRE (VO):
That defiance forged fierce talent. Like Edward “Magents” Motale, a future 1996 Africa Cup of Nations winner.

EDWARD INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:13:22,866 → 00:13:54,100
Edward: When Steve came closer, he played a big role. He brought change — started requiring black players...
CLAIRE (VO):
The field was his battleground. And every match, a test of will.

EDWARD INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:10:06,866 → 00:10:15,366
The stubbornness I learned at Arcadia — from apartheid — made me strong and cheeky... Every time I played... they’d remind me how black I am. But I stood firm. I told myself, “Black is beautiful.”

CLAIRE (VO):
For others, Arcadia was simply a family. A sanctuary where only football mattered. Like former goalkeeper Deshi Bhaktawer, who stood as the family's last line of defence.

DESHI INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:03:07,200 – 00:03:11,300
Deshi: And at that time, it was a time in South Africa where there was segregation... for me, it was all about football.

(The Collapse: The Betrayal)
CLAIRE (VO):
The legacy continued into a new South Africa. The stadium became a home for Banyana Banyana.
FRAN HILTON-SMITH INTERVIEW
00:04:56,000 – 00:05:08,166
We used to play there from 2000 to 2008... We even drew with Nigeria there once — that was a historical moment…

VO
For Fran Hilton-Smith, a pioneer who fought for decades to build women’s football from nothing, the loss of a talent incubator like Caledonian is a familiar frustration.

FRAN HILTON SMITH INTERVIEW
00:04:28,166 – 00:04:33,900
Family. And that’s what it was all about. The Caledonian — it was a family affair.
00:04:47,166 – 00:04:56,000
So it really was an outing. And certainly for me, in women’s football, it’s a major part of the history of Banyana.

CLAIRE (VO):
But the political battles over the stadium’s fate were already lost. The legends point a direct finger at the politicians, they say erased their history.

EDWARD INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:16:21,000 → 00:16:25,866
There were fights for power, ownership. When the DA took over, they wanted to dismantle it and make a park. We refused... That stadium has been there for over a hundred years. You can’t destroy that history.
CLAIRE PTC
00:01:09,866 → 00:01:12,433
The story of this demolished stadium asks a tough question: if we could find the heroes back then, why can’t we protect the systems that create them today?


(The Legacy: The Future)

CLAIRE (VO):
The factory is gone. But the architect is still at work. Steve Coetzee has started from scratch.

Visuals: Kids playing football at Capital City FC.
STEVE INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:12:04,700 --> 00:12:13,200
Steve: Arcadia Shepherds still exist today, playing in local leagues... They've been promised the Caledonian once it's restored - if that ever happens.

CLAIRE (VO):
His new mission is Capital City FC – a conscious attempt to rebuild the dream, far from the politics and decay of the past. That same model once produced a Bafana captain. Bongani Khumalo was in his pre-teens when he met Steve.

BONGANI KHUMALO/FORMER BAFANA CAPTAIN INTERVIEW UPSOUND
Bongani Khumalo: So I met Coach Steve when I was 12, in 1998. I’d gone to Arcadia Shepherds for a trial.

CLAIRE (VO):
Now, both men agree on the solution.
STEVE INTERVIEW
00:18:09,666 --> 00:18:27,300
Steve: We need better coach education and mentorship. Better coaches make better players. That's the foundation.
BONGANI INTERVIEW UPSOUND
00:05:12,266 - 00:05:19,133
Bongani Khumalo: If we can get people with the right hearts, like Steve, and plant the money down there, by the time these kids reach the fans' TV sets, you'll see more quality football.

CLOSING SEQUENCE
Visuals: Kids playing football at Capital City FC.
CLAIRE (VO):
The fight for the next generation is on. But the question remains: Is South Africa still failing its future stars?


PROMOS


PROMO1
CLAIRE PTC :
"Generations of football royalty are united in grief..., but from the rubble, a new rebellion is born."
FRAN HILTON-SMITH UPSOUND (Hopeful, visionary):
"We hope that they will rebuild something at that centre... It's a perfect venue, and people can access it."
CLAIRE VO:
The fight for the next generation is on as we examine the legacy of a legendary football factory.

Like former goalkeeper Deshi Bhaktawer, who stood as the family's last line of defence. DESHI INTERVIEW UPSOUND 00:03:07,200 – 00:03:11,300 Deshi: And at that time, it was a time in South Africa where there was segregation... for me, it was all about football. (The Collapse: The Betrayal) CLAIRE (VO): The legacy continued into a new South Africa. The stadium became a home for Banyana Banyana. FRAN HILTON-SMITH INTERVIEW 00:04:56,000 – 00:05:08,166 We used to play there from 2000 to 2008... We even drew with Nigeria there once — that was a historical moment… VO For Fran Hilton-Smith, a pioneer who fought for decades to build women’s football from nothing, the loss of a talent incubator like Caledonian is a familiar frustration. FRAN HILTON SMITH INTERVIEW 00:04:28,166 – 00:04:33,900 Family. And that’s what it was all about. The Caledonian — it was a family affair. 00:04:47,166 – 00:04:56,000 So it really was an outing. And certainly for me, in women’s football, it’s a major part of the history of Banyana. CLAIRE (VO): But the political battles over the stadium’s fate were already lost. The legends point a direct finger at the politicians, they say erased their history. EDWARD INTERVIEW UPSOUND 00:16:21,000 → 00:16:25,866 There were fights for power, ownership. When the DA took over, they wanted to dismantle it and make a park. We refused... That stadium has been there for over a hundred years. You can’t destroy that history. CLAIRE PTC 00:01:09,866 → 00:01:12,433 The story of this demolished stadium asks a tough question: if we could find the heroes back then, why can’t we protect the systems that create them today? (The Legacy: The Future) CLAIRE (VO): The factory is gone. But the architect is still at work. Steve Coetzee has started from scratch. Visuals: Kids playing football at Capital City FC. STEVE INTERVIEW UPSOUND 00:12:04,700 --> 00:12:13,200 Steve: Arcadia Shepherds still exist today, playing in local leagues... They've been promised the Caledonian once it's restored - if that ever happens. CLAIRE (VO): His new mission is Capital City FC – a conscious attempt to rebuild the dream, far from the politics and decay of the past. That same model once produced a Bafana captain. Bongani Khumalo was in his pre-teens when he met Steve. BONGANI KHUMALO/FORMER BAFANA CAPTAIN INTERVIEW UPSOUND Bongani Khumalo: So I met Coach Steve when I was 12, in 1998. I’d gone to Arcadia Shepherds for a trial. CLAIRE (VO): Now, both men agree on the solution. STEVE INTERVIEW 00:18:09,666 --> 00:18:27,300 Steve: We need better coach education and mentorship. Better coaches make better players. That's the foundation. BONGANI INTERVIEW UPSOUND 00:05:12,266 - 00:05:19,133 Bongani Khumalo: If we can get people with the right hearts, like Steve, and plant the money down there, by the time these kids reach the fans' TV sets, you'll see more quality football. CLOSING SEQUENCE Visuals: Kids playing football at Capital City FC. CLAIRE (VO): The fight for the next generation is on. But the question remains: Is South Africa still failing its future stars? PROMOS PROMO1 CLAIRE PTC : "Generations of football royalty are united in grief..., but from the rubble, a new rebellion is born." FRAN HILTON-SMITH UPSOUND (Hopeful, visionary): "We hope that they will rebuild something at that centre... It's a perfect venue, and people can access it." CLAIRE VO: The fight for the next generation is on as we examine the legacy of a legendary football factory.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Arcadia Shepherds Football Club – produced legends, racially integrated. National talent incubator. Now lies in ruins, homeless people live there. Used to be a beautiful place
metadata.Summary: Arcadia Shepherds was a national talent incubator that produced legends like Mark Fish and Edward Motale. Today, its grounds are a derelict ruin. What forces – financial, political, societal – conspired to destroy South Africa’s most potent unofficial development machine? This is the mystery we will solve.
metadata.Further information: The Investigative Journey We Will Take the Viewer On 1. The Crime Scene: A Factory in Ruins We open at the Caledonian Stadium. Through stark drone shots, we show the viewer the "body"—the overgrown fields and crumbling structures. This is the factory floor, now silent. The Question Posed Visually: How did this place, which assembled Bafana Bafana stars, end up like this? 2. The Blueprint: How the Factory Worked We showcase the "Golden Age" with rich archives and nostalgic interviews. The Architect: Coach Steve Coetzee explains his methods and his eye for talent. The Products: Exclusive interviews with Edward Motale (1996 Afcon winner) and former goalkeeper Deshi Bhaktawer. They are living proof of the factory's output, testifying to the unique environment that created them. The Defiance: We highlight the pioneering signing of Vincent Julius and the visual evolution of the team, showing a club ahead of its time. 3. The Investigation: Who or What Killed the Factory? This is the core of our investigation, providing concrete answers to the central question. Suspect 1: Political Sabotage: The fateful Kaiser Chiefs match that gave the apartheid government a pretext to close their ground. Steve Coetzee explicitly identifies this as the beginning of the end. Suspect 2: Administrative Failure: The decision by club leadership to sell out to Dynamos, despite players offering to play for free. This points to internal failure and a loss of vision. Suspect 3: Systemic Neglect: We bring in Fran Hilton-Smith, former SAFA Technical Director. She provides the expert, systemic perspective on why grassroots incubators like Arcadia were allowed to die and what this says about the failures of the official development structure. 4. The Verdict: The Legacy of a Lost Factory We return to the ruins of the Caledonian. The visuals now carry the weight of the answers we've uncovered. We see Steve Coetzee, now a CAF/SAFA coach educator, trying to rebuild a similar model with his new club, Capital City—a small, hopeful effort against a tide of systemic challenges. The Final Answer: The factory was killed by a combination of political pressure, internal mismanagement, and a system that failed to protect its most valuable assets. Its death left a hole in South Africa's football soul.
